To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

insulin resistance induced by overexpression of bovine GH gene in transgenic mice is associated with a decrease in hepatic insulin receptor number and a concomitant increase in autophosphorylative activity.

in the liver of PEPCK-bigh transgenic mice the number of InsR and the InsR autophyosphorylation activity are increased in response to the normalization of insulinemia, while the InsR concentration and affinity are unaltered.

insulin receptor concentration and tyrosine kinase activities are increased by insulin in transgenic mice that overexpress the bovine growth hormone gene, and that this effect is independent of the presence of serine/threonines in the beta-subunit.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the early steps of the insulin signaling cascade in the liver of insulin-resistant transgenic mice overproducing bGH.
the study of the early steps of the insulin signal transduction pathway in transgenic mice.
the role of hyperinsulinism in the pathogenesis of hepatic insulin resistance induced by chronic exposure to high levels of GH.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hyperinsulinemia, in the presence of elevated growth hormone levels, is responsible for the alterations in InsR concentration and autophophorylation activity in bGH transgenic mouse liver.

the changes in insulin receptor concentration and insulin receptor autophosphorylating activity observed in the liver of transgenic bGH mice are secondary to hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia, and that they do not result from the chronic elevation of GH levels.

the alterations in the InsR concentration and autophos-phorylation in the liver of PEPCK-bigh transgenic mice are secondary to hyper-insulinemia, and are not due to the chronic exposure to elevated GH levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

insulin resistance in transgenic mice is due to the combined effect of high GH and high insulin blood levels, with the latter being responsible for downregulating InsR number and increasing InsR autophorylation activity.
the alterations in insulin signal transduction detected in the liver of PEPCK-bHG transgenic mice are secondary to hyper-insulinemia.
in transgenic mice the hyperinsulinemia compensates the insulin resistance due to GH overexpression.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the alterations in insulin receptor number and autophosorylation activity observed in the livers of transgenic PEPCK-bovine growth hormone (GH) mice are secondary to the high insulin levels induced by GH overexpression, and are not directly related to the high GH levels themselves.

insulin receptor autophosphorylating activity in the transgenic mouse is regulated by insulin levels, and that the insulin resistance observed in the transgenic animal is a direct consequence of hyperinsulinism.
hyperinsulinemia is a major determinant of insulin resistance in this model.
